[curious, lively, starts speaking immediately] In nineteen eighty-three, the alarms said: missiles incoming. One Soviet officer had only minutes to decide what to do. His name was Stanislav Petrov, the duty officer at a warning center. The screens showed one launch, then five. His orders: report an attack up the chain. That could have triggered a nuclear counterstrike. But something felt off. A real first strike would mean hundreds of missiles, not five. Ground radar saw nothing. He called it a false alarm. He was right: the satellites had mistaken sunlight on high clouds for launches. Five missiles that were never there.
